assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reshaped international trade theory and empirics. It created the standard framework for gains from trade, reallocation and the extensive margin, and it spread into macroeconomics, productivity and industrial organisation. The conceptual break from representative-firm models is clear and the policy relevance is high.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central paper. Helpman is credited for the broader firm-level trade programme and for work that links it to the data, including with Melitz and Yeaple. Redding is a significant contributor to quantitative extensions, but the core idea is concentrated in Melitz and Helpman. Related precursors, such as Bernard and Jensen on exporter facts, may complicate credit.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of testing, extension and teaching. The framework is a standard part of graduate curricula and has been repeatedly confirmed empirically.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the discovery as a refinement of the new trade theory already recognised in 2008 rather than a new field.
Credit allocation among Melitz, Helpman and Redding, and the role of empirical precursors.
My knowledge of the later quantitative literature may be incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients demand estimation (BLP) and dynamic oligopoly estimation changed how demand, market power, mergers and competition policy are studied empirically. The methods are used constantly in academia, antitrust practice and industry, and they combine theory with identification and computation.
assessment.attribution: The BLP contributions (Berry; Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes) are well defined. Pakes also has dynamic-game and estimation work (Ericson-Pakes, and Pakes with Benkard and others). Bresnahan and Reiss are important for early empirical IO and entry models, and Levin and Benkard are significant but more peripheral. The list is large, so a three-person cap forces hard choices.
assessment.maturity: The BLP method dates from the mid-1990s and has been validated, extended and widely adopted over three decades, so timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan or Reiss should displace Levinsohn, or be added, on grounds of priority.
Ongoing methodological debates about the sensitivity of demand estimates and the credibility of structural models.
Fit with the committee's recent emphasis on design-based empirical work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal-rigidity microfoundations, the New Keynesian framework and rule-based monetary policy analysis underpin modern central banking and inflation targeting. Staggered contracts and pricing, the Taylor rule and the policy-analysis framework have had enormous practical and theoretical influence.
assessment.attribution: The credit is spread across many contributors, including Calvo (time-dependent pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and rules), Woodford (the integrated NK framework), Galí, Gertler, Clarida, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets. The three named are the most defensible for foundational priority and framing, but any selection omits central figures. Sargent-Sims (2011) and the 2022 prize covered adjacent ground.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with decades of use and validation. The 2008–2022 experience tested the framework, both supporting its core and exposing limits on the zero lower bound and heterogeneity.
uncertainties: A three-laureate cap forces a contested selection from a field with many essential contributors.
Overlap with earlier macro prizes (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims) might reduce its perceived novelty.
The framework's performance after the pandemic inflation is debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bringing sufficient-statistics optimal tax theory together with the empirical elasticity of taxable income gave tax design a quantitatively operational framework. It also showed how behavioural responses, avoidance and evasion matter for revenue and welfare. The policy impact on income and top-rate taxation debates is large.
assessment.attribution: Slemrod is the key figure on taxable income, tax avoidance and the empirical public finance tradition. Saez is a central figure in optimal-tax theory and in empirical estimation. Chetty and Stantcheva have important contributions, but they are more recent and in part overlap with other candidates (mobility, behavioural public economics). Feldstein's foundational work on taxable income is not listed, and Mirrlees and Diamond are already recognised.
assessment.maturity: The elasticity-of-taxable-income literature has matured over about 30 years. Parts of the empirical evidence remain contested, with sensitivity to identification and methodology.
uncertainties: The elasticity estimates are debated, and identification concerns remain.
Saez's appearance in several candidate bundles complicates distinct credit.
Feldstein's priority cannot be reflected, given his death.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification changed how inference is framed. It asks what can be learned under credible, weak assumptions rather than relying on strong assumptions for point identification. It is conceptually deep and applies across empirical fields, including treatment effects, discrete-choice games and policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the clear originator, with bounds and the decision-theoretic framing from the late 1980s onward. Tamer is a major contributor to modern moment-inequality theory and applications. Molinari is a leading contemporary contributor on inference. The credit is relatively clean around Manski, with the others as developers of the framework.
assessment.maturity: Foundations date back about 35 years, and the inference toolkit has matured over the last 20. Adoption in applied work is real but less pervasive than for the design-based methods already honoured in 2021.
uncertainties: Whether applied adoption is broad enough to be seen as transformative for empirical practice.
Whether the committee prefers to honour Manski alone, or with a developer, since Tamer and Molinari work in a younger tradition.
Overlap with the 2021 emphasis on identification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based framework, skill-biased and routine-biased technical change, and the empirical analysis of labour-market polarisation and trade exposure transformed understanding of wage inequality, automation and labour demand. The questions are of the first order, and the policy impact on debates about globalisation and technology is large.
assessment.attribution: Autor and Katz anchor the technology and wage-structure work (with Katz-Murphy and Autor-Levy-Murnane). Dorn and Hanson are central to the China-shock empirics, and Acemoglu-Restrepo, who share the task framework, are not on this bundle. Acemoglu was recognised in 2024 for institutions, which may lessen the sense of an open slot.
assessment.maturity: Substantial time has passed, and the results are well replicated. There is ongoing debate about magnitudes, mechanisms and the role of trade versus technology, as well as the more recent AI-related extensions.
uncertainties: Credit split between the technology strand and the trade-shock strand.
The absence of key co-developers, notably Acemoglu, from the credited set.
Open debate over the magnitude of the effects.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance brought legal origins and investor protection into comparative finance and growth. It launched a very large literature on institutions and financial development, and the questions it raised on corporate governance and ownership are important. The influence across finance, law and political economy has been substantial.
assessment.attribution: The core cross-country papers are by La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny (LLSV). A three-person cap would force Vishny out despite his coauthorship, and Shleifer also has the behavioural-finance and limits-of-arbitrage work. The credit structure is therefore awkward.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with 25+ years of replication and critique. The legal-origins thesis itself has been challenged on measurement, endogeneity and causal interpretation, and the central claims have been qualified.
uncertainties: Persistent challenges to the identification and robustness of the legal-origins results.
The four-way LLSV credit, and the three-laureate limit.
I work in a neighbouring field, so my familiarity with the core evidence is closer, and I have tried to apply the same criteria used for other fields.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A systematic theory and empirics of how constitutions, electoral rules and political institutions shape fiscal policy, redistribution and state capacity. It brought political economics into the mainstream and linked institutional design to measurable economic outcomes.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the clear authors of the unifying framework, in papers and in their book Political Economics (2000), and of the empirical work on constitutions. Besley is a major contributor on state capacity, accountability and the political economy of development. The pair has the stronger claim to the framework, though Besley's inclusion would be defensible.
assessment.maturity: The framework and findings have developed over 30 years. The causal interpretation of the constitutional results is contested, and the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity may reduce the perceived room for a closely related prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 institutions prize.
Whether Besley should be included, given the cap on laureates.
Persson's long association with the Committee may be seen as a conflict, which is disclosed but not adjudicated here.
